title: Level 11: UART Receive with Interrupt-Driven Circular Buffer
aim: To configure the ATmega328P's USART0 to receive incoming serial bytes interrupt-driven via RXC0 ISR, storing them in a circular (ring) buffer for non-blocking processing by the main loop.
objective: Understand UART receive mechanism (RXEN0, RXC0 flag, UDR0 read), interrupt-driven RX design, circular buffer data structure, volatile shared variables, and the critical section problem when accessing shared buffers between ISR and main code.
theory:
UART Receive — The Challenge

Transmitting data is simple — you decide when to send. Receiving is harder: bytes arrive at unpredictable times driven by the sender. If the main loop is busy when a byte arrives and doesn't read UDR0 before the next byte arrives, the DOR0 (Data OverRun) flag is set and the byte is lost. The solution: use the RX Complete Interrupt (RXC0) to immediately capture each byte as it arrives.

RX Complete Interrupt

When a full UART frame has been received and is ready in UDR0, the hardware sets the RXC0 flag in UCSR0A and fires the ISR(USART_RX_vect) if RXCIE0 is enabled in UCSR0B. Inside the ISR, reading UDR0 returns the received byte AND clears the RXC0 flag. This must happen before the next byte finishes arriving (within one frame time = 1.04 ms at 9600 baud).

Circular Buffer (Ring Buffer)

An ISR must execute extremely fast. We should not process the received byte in the ISR — just store it. A circular buffer is perfect: a fixed-size array with two pointers (head and tail) that wrap around:

  • HEAD — where the ISR writes new bytes
  • TAIL — where main loop reads bytes
  • Buffer is empty when HEAD == TAIL
  • Buffer is full when (HEAD + 1) % SIZE == TAIL

The ISR advances HEAD. The main loop advances TAIL. Since only the ISR writes HEAD and only main reads TAIL, the buffer is naturally thread-safe for this single-producer, single-consumer pattern — without needing to disable interrupts.

Error Flags — FE0, DOR0, UPE0

Before reading UDR0, check the error flags in UCSR0A:

  • FE0 (Frame Error) — Stop bit was 0 (expected 1). Baud mismatch or line glitch.
  • DOR0 (Data OverRun) — A new frame arrived before UDR0 was read. Character lost.
  • UPE0 (Parity Error) — Received parity doesn't match. Line noise or incompatible parity setting.

These flags are cleared by reading UDR0, so check them first in the ISR.

volatile and Memory Barriers

All circular buffer variables shared between the ISR and main must be declared volatile to prevent the compiler from optimizing away reads/writes from SRAM. When checking buffer state in a critical section, use cli()/sei() pairs to atomically read 8-bit indices (which are not atomic on AVR if they span multiple instructions with 16-bit types).

pretest.question: Which flag indicates UART received data is ready in UDR0?
pretest.explanation: RXC0 (RX Complete flag, bit 7 of UCSR0A) is set when a received byte is ready in UDR0. It clears automatically when UDR0 is read.

pretest.question: Which bit in UCSR0B enables the UART receive interrupt?
pretest.explanation: RXCIE0 (RX Complete Interrupt Enable, bit 7 of UCSR0B) enables the USART_RX_vect ISR to fire when RXC0 is set.

pretest.question: What ISR vector handles USART0 RX in AVR?
pretest.explanation: USART_RX_vect fires when a byte has been fully received and is available in UDR0. It maps to vector address 0x0012 in the ATmega328P interrupt table.

pretest.question: What is the DOR0 flag and when is it set?
options: Data Ready — set when TX complete
Data OverRun — set when a new frame arrives before UDR0 was read
pretest.explanation: DOR0 (Data OverRun) in UCSR0A is set when the receive shift register receives a second byte before the first was read from UDR0. The second byte replaces the first — data is lost.

pretest.question: In a circular buffer with SIZE=16, if HEAD=15 and TAIL=0, is the buffer full or has 1 slot?
options: 1 slot — HEAD is at 15, TAIL is at 0
pretest.explanation: Buffer full condition: (HEAD + 1) % SIZE == TAIL → (15+1)%16 = 0 == TAIL(0) → FULL. One slot is sacrificed to distinguish full from empty.

pretest.question: Why must circular buffer index variables be declared 'volatile'?
options: Prevent compiler from caching them in registers, ensuring ISR and main always see each other's updates
pretest.explanation: Without volatile, the compiler may keep the index in a CPU register and never reload from SRAM, so either main or the ISR sees stale values.

pretest.question: How many bytes does UART buffer hold between ISR captures if operating at 9600 baud and the MCU processes 100 bytes in 10 ms?
options: 1 byte arrives every 1.04 ms, so ~10 bytes approach in 10 ms — need buffer >= 10
pretest.explanation: At 9600 baud 8N1: one byte takes 10 bits × (1/9600) = 1.04 ms. In 10 ms, ~9.6 bytes could arrive. The circular buffer must be big enough to hold these during peak load.

pretest.question: Why shouldn't you call _delay_ms() or heavy processing inside the RX ISR?
options: No access to delay.h in ISRs
Blocking ISR prevents other interrupts and delays UDR0 reads, risking DOR0 data overrun
pretest.explanation: If the ISR blocks during the 1.04 ms before the next byte arrives, the hardware will overrun and data is lost. ISRs must read UDR0 and return immediately.

pretest.question: The main loop checks if buffer is not empty by comparing:
pretest.explanation: Buffer not empty: HEAD != TAIL. Empty: HEAD == TAIL. The main loop reads from TAIL and increments it, while ISR writes to HEAD and increments it.

pretest.question: What does the RXEN0 bit in UCSR0B do?
options: Enables the USART receiver — takes control of PD0 (RX pin)
pretest.explanation: RXEN0 (Receiver Enable, bit 4 of UCSR0B) enables the USART receiver hardware and overrides PD0's DDR/PORT for RX function.

procedure: Configure USART0 for 9600 baud 8N1 as in Exp 10: set UBRR0, UCSR0C=0x06. Enable receiver and transmitter, plus the RX Complete interrupt: UCSR0B = (1<<RXEN0) | (1<<TXEN0) | (1<<RXCIE0);.
Enable global interrupts: sei();. The UART RX interrupt is now armed — any incoming byte will trigger the ISR within 1 frame time.

Write the RX ISR: check errors first (FE0, DOR0 in UCSR0A), then always read UDR0 (clears flags): ISR(USART_RX_vect) { uint8_t status = UCSR0A; uint8_t byte = UDR0; if (!(status & ((1<<FE0)|(1<<DOR0)|(1<<UPE0)))) { uint8_t next = (rxHead + 1) & (BUF_SIZE-1); if (next != rxTail) { rxBuf[rxHead] = byte; rxHead = next; } } }

Write a buffer-read helper for the main loop: int16_t uart_read(void) { if (rxHead == rxTail) return -1; uint8_t b = rxBuf[rxTail]; rxTail = (rxTail + 1) & (BUF_SIZE-1); return b; }. Returns -1 if no data.

In the main loop: while(1) { int16_t b = uart_read(); if (b >= 0) { uart_tx((uint8_t)b); } }. This echo loop reads each received byte from the buffer and transmits it back — a standard UART loopback test.
Connect the Arduino to a serial terminal at 9600 baud. Type characters — they should echo back immediately. Test buffer overflow behaviour by sending a burst of characters quickly.
Verify with a logic analyser or oscilloscope on PD0 (RX) that each incoming frame (start bit + 8 data bits + stop bit) is correctly framed at the expected symbol rate.

posttest.question: What is the maximum safe data rate at which the MCU can receive without needing a buffer (direct ISR processing)?
options: Rate at which each ISR completes before next byte arrives
posttest.explanation: Without a buffer, ISR must complete within 1 frame time. At 9600 baud that's ~1.04 ms. If ISR processing takes less than that, no buffer is needed. For faster rates or heavier ISR processing, a buffer is essential.

posttest.question: Why is a power-of-two buffer size preferred?
options: Modulo operation becomes AND with (SIZE-1) — much faster on 8-bit MCU with no HW divider
posttest.explanation: The ATmega328P has no hardware divider. % with a power-of-two is compiled to a bitwise AND (1 cycle), while arbitrary modulo requires a software division routine (many cycles).

posttest.question: What is a frame error (FE0) and what causes it?
options: Expected stop bit was 0 (logic LOW) — baud mismatch, noise, or wrong parity
posttest.explanation: A frame error occurs when the stop bit is sampled as LOW instead of HIGH. The most common cause is baud rate mismatch between transmitter and receiver.

posttest.question: To re-enable RX interrupt after a cli()-protected section in main, what must you call?
posttest.explanation: cli() clears the global I-bit in SREG. sei() restores it. You don't need to re-enable RXCIE0 — it was never disabled. Only the global interrupt was masked.

posttest.question: What is the difference between USART_RX_vect and USART_UDRE_vect?
options: USART_RX_vect fires when byte received; USART_UDRE_vect fires when TX buffer ready for next byte
posttest.explanation: USART_RX_vect = RX Complete interrupt (byte received, RXC0 set). USART_UDRE_vect = USART Data Register Empty interrupt (TX buffer ready, UDRE0 set) — used for interrupt-driven TX.

posttest.question: What does the SREG register contain?
options: CPU status flags and global interrupt enable (I-bit)
posttest.explanation: SREG holds the CPU flags (C, Z, N, V, H, S, T) and the I-bit (global interrupt enable).

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
posttest.explanation: WDT auto-resets MCU when not periodically cleared — essential firmware safety net.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has Port B, C, D only.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM when power is removed?
In an ISR, what variable keyword prevents compiler optimization that could miss ISR updates?
posttest.explanation: volatile forces the compiler to always read/write from SRAM, ensuring the ISR and main always see current values.

feedback: Incredible! Interrupt-driven UART with circular buffers is used in every serious embedded product — from Bluetooth stacks to GNSS parsers to industrial field buses. You now understand how to build robust, non-blocking communication at the register level.
